AI4MOBILITY · MULTIMODAL FUSION

Fifteen fusion papers, and the recipe most of them share

How do published models combine cameras, LiDAR, text, audio, maps and V2X messages? Each card below shows one paper’s architecture figure, answers the same five questions in plain words, and draws the paper as a who-reads-whom table (how to read it is just below). At the end: what the standard architecture looks like, and what still varies.

Reading the who-reads-whom table
  • Rows ask (↓), columns answer (→): the row’s queries read the column’s keys and values.
  • self: a stream reads itself · cross-attention · gate: cross-attention scaled by a learned gate
  • mask: attention limited by geometry, time order or a rule · conv: combined without attention · off
  • cells outlined together share one softmax: those streams compete for one budget of weight.

The papers

Filter by family, or jump to a year. A paper can belong to more than one family.

2019 ViLBERT MulT
2021 CLIP ViLT Perceiver and Perceiver IO MBT TransFuser
2022 Flamingo BEVFormer V2X-ViT Wayformer BEVFusion
2023 BLIP-2 LLaVA
2024 Chameleon

ViLBERT

Lu, Batra, Parikh & Lee · NeurIPS 2019 · arXiv:1908.02265
Two towers and pairwise
Streams
Image regions from an object detector; the words of a caption or question.
Where they meet
Mid: the text first runs through several BERT layers alone; the image regions go straight to the first co-attention layer.
Who asks
Both. Each stream keeps its own queries and reads the other stream’s keys and values (“co-attention”).
One softmax?
Separate: two attention blocks, one per direction.
Stream tag
No stream-type vector. Each image region carries a 5-number box position.

Two BERT-like towers, one for image regions and one for words, that trade keys and values in co-attention layers. The image side asks the words and the word side asks the image, each with its own weights and its own softmax. Because the text runs alone first, its representation can be computed once and cached before fusion.

What they found
  • Against a single-stream version of itself (one shared sequence), ViLBERT scored 70.55 vs 68.85 on VQA test-dev and 72.34 vs 69.21 on RefCOCO+ (Table 1).

For mobility: Two very different streams you want to keep apart but let talk both ways: a dashcam stream and an incident-report text.

MulT (Multimodal Transformer)

Tsai et al. · ACL 2019 · arXiv:1906.00295
Two towers and pairwise
Streams
Language (word vectors), vision (facial action units) and audio (acoustic features), for sentiment and emotion.
Where they meet
From the first block. Each stream gets only a 1-D convolution and a position code, on its own clock.
Who asks
The target stream asks; keys and values come from the source stream’s low-level features.
One softmax?
Separate: six directed crossmodal blocks, one per ordered pair. Outputs with the same target are concatenated, then self-attention.
Stream tag
No stream-type vector: each stream stays its own sequence.

Built for streams that are not aligned in time: words, face and voice arrive at different rates. Instead of forcing them onto one clock, each stream asks each other stream directly, in its own block.

What they found
  • On unaligned CMU-MOSEI, binary accuracy 81.6 for MulT vs 78.9 for an early-fusion transformer that concatenates the three streams, and 78.6 for late fusion (Table 4).

For mobility: Streams on different clocks are the norm here: BSMs at 10 Hz, CAN at 100 Hz, video at 30 fps, loop data in 20-second or 5-minute bins.

CLIP

Radford et al. · ICML 2021 · arXiv:2103.00020
Two towers and pairwise
Streams
Images and their captions: 400 million pairs.
Where they meet
Late: never inside the network. Each encoder ends in one vector, and the two vectors meet in a cosine similarity.
Who asks
Nobody: there is no cross-attention between the streams.
One softmax?
No attention across streams. (Training uses a softmax over the batch of image–caption pairs, which is a loss, not attention.)
Stream tag
Not needed: the streams never share a sequence.

Two encoders trained so that matching images and captions point the same way. Each side can be encoded once and stored, so searching millions of images with a sentence is fast.

What they found
  • Zero-shot ImageNet accuracy 76.2% (Table 1).
  • The ViLT paper later showed the limit: a dot product of CLIP’s two vectors scored 50.99 on NLVR2, a two-choice reasoning test: chance level.

For mobility: Searching a camera archive with a sentence (“bus blocking the right lane”): late fusion to retrieve, a cross-attention model to re-rank.

ViLT

Kim, Son & Kim · ICML 2021 · arXiv:2102.03334
One sequence
Streams
Image patches and words.
Where they meet
Early: from layer 1, in one sequence.
Who asks
Every token asks every token.
One softmax?
One softmax over words and patches together.
Stream tag
Yes: a learned “modal-type embedding” is added to every token, plus position embeddings.

No heavy per-stream encoder: words get a word embedding, image patches a single linear projection, each token gets its stream’s type vector, and one 12-layer transformer reads the whole sequence. The authors chose one stream because two towers add parameters.

What they found
  • About 15 ms per example vs about 900 ms for UNITER-Base, which needs an object detector; VQAv2 70.33 vs 72.70 (Table 2). Much faster, slightly less accurate.
  • 87.4 M parameters and 55.9 GFLOPs vs 274.3 M and 958.1 GFLOPs for a ViLBERT-style model (Table 6).

For mobility: When the latency of a roadside unit matters more than the last point of accuracy, try a light single-stream model first.

Perceiver and Perceiver IO

Jaegle et al. · ICML 2021 · ICLR 2022 · arXiv:2103.03206 · arXiv:2107.14795
Queries and bottlenecks
Streams
Any: images, point clouds, and video with audio (AudioSet).
Where they meet
At the first cross-attention: “modalities are fused at input”. There is no per-stream encoder.
Who asks
A small learned latent array asks; every input is a key and value.
One softmax?
One softmax over all inputs of all streams.
Stream tag
Yes: a learned modality-specific code is appended to each input; it doubles as a position code.

Instead of every input reading every input, a fixed set of latent vectors reads all the inputs, then the latents work among themselves. The cost grows with the number of inputs, not with its square, so adding layers does not get more expensive as inputs grow. Perceiver IO adds output queries, one per answer you want, that read the latents.

What they found
  • AudioSet, audio + video: 43.5 mAP (raw audio) and 43.2 (spectrogram) (Table 3). The authors note this is still below the best system that uses separate models and late fusion.
  • Perceiver IO, spectrogram + video: 44.9 vs 43.6 for Perceiver (Table 10).

For mobility: A fixed set of latents is a natural hub for an intersection; the lane-anchor tokens of the flexible-fusion slides are latents tied to the road.

MBT (Attention Bottlenecks)

Nagrani et al. · NeurIPS 2021 · arXiv:2107.00135
Queries and bottlenecks
Streams
Video frames and the audio spectrogram, for video classification.
Where they meet
Mid: after L_f layers of their own. The best model starts fusing at layer 8 of 12.
Who asks
Each stream’s tokens plus 4 shared bottleneck tokens attend together; the bottleneck copies are then averaged across streams.
One softmax?
One softmax per stream, over that stream plus the bottleneck. Video and audio never read each other directly.
Stream tag
No type vector: separate input projections and a separate class token per stream.

Let each stream build its own features first, then force all cross-stream information through a handful of shared tokens. The narrow channel is cheap and, in their tests, more accurate than letting everything read everything.

What they found
  • Moving from late fusion to MBT: mini-AudioSet 41.80 → 43.92 mAP; Epic-Kitchens 37.90 → 43.40 (Table 9).
  • Four bottleneck tokens add “negligible extra computation over a late fusion model”; at early fusion, bottlenecks beat full cross-attention by over 2 mAP at less than half the cost.

For mobility: A cheap channel between two heavy encoders, such as two cameras, or a camera and a radar on an embedded computer.

TransFuser

Prakash, Chitta & Geiger; Chitta et al. · CVPR 2021 · TPAMI 2023 · arXiv:2104.09224 · arXiv:2205.15997
One sequenceDriving and V2X
Streams
A front camera image and LiDAR drawn as a bird’s-eye-view image, for end-to-end driving in the CARLA simulator.
Where they meet
Mid, at every scale: one transformer at each of four resolutions, starting at the first ResNet stage.
Who asks
Every image token and every LiDAR token asks all tokens of both streams.
One softmax?
One softmax: “these features are stacked together to form a sequence”. The outputs are added back into each branch.
Stream tag
A learned position embedding over the stacked sequence; no separate stream-type vector.

Two convolutional branches, one per sensor, that meet four times on the way up. At each meeting the feature maps are shrunk to 8 × 8 tokens per stream, stacked into one sequence, mixed by self-attention, and handed back to their branches.

What they found
  • CARLA Town05 Long driving score 33.15 vs 31.30 for late fusion and 25.30 for geometry-based fusion; the abstract reports 76% fewer collisions than geometry-based fusion (CVPR, Table 1a).
  • Fusing at only one scale: 41.94 vs 59.99 for all four (CVPR, Table 2). The journal version adds 17% runtime over late fusion: 27.6 vs 23.5 ms per frame.

For mobility: The closest published cousin of a camera + LiDAR (or camera + radar) model for an automated vehicle or a smart intersection.

Flamingo

Alayrac et al. · NeurIPS 2022 · arXiv:2204.14198
Bridges to frozen modelsQueries and bottlenecks
Streams
Images or video interleaved with text; output is text.
Where they meet
Mid: new gated cross-attention layers sit before frozen language-model blocks, from the first block on (every block in the 3B model; every 4th or 7th block in larger ones).
Who asks
Text tokens ask; keys and values are 64 visual tokens from the Perceiver Resampler. A mask lets each text token read only the most recent image.
One softmax?
Separate: the text-to-vision block is its own attention, apart from the language model’s self-attention.
Stream tag
Markers in the text (an image tag) instead of a type vector.

Two pretrained models are kept frozen: a vision encoder and a large language model. Flamingo adds the new layers only. Each new layer’s output is multiplied by tanh of a learned number that starts at 0, so at the start of training the language model behaves exactly as before, and the vision path opens as it proves useful.

What they found
  • Removing the tanh gate dropped the overall score of the 3B model from 70.7 to 66.5, with training instabilities (Table 3).
  • Inserting the layers only every fourth block trained 66% faster for a 1.9% lower overall score.

For mobility: Adding a new sensor to a model that already works, such as a driver camera to a validated road-camera model, without disturbing it at first.

BEVFormer

Li et al. · ECCV 2022 · arXiv:2203.17270
Queries and bottlenecksDriving and V2X
Streams
Six surround cameras (nuScenes), plus the model’s own bird’s-eye-view map from the previous moment.
Where they meet
In each of 6 encoder layers: temporal self-attention first, then spatial cross-attention.
Who asks
A 200 × 200 grid of learned BEV queries (0.512 m cells) asks: the previous BEV map, aligned for ego-motion, and the camera features.
One softmax?
Not a single dot-product softmax: deformable attention samples a few points around each cell’s projected 3-D reference points, with learned weights; views are handled separately and averaged.
Stream tag
A learnable position embedding on the BEV queries; geometry enters through each camera’s projection, so a cell reads only the views it lands in.

Each cell of a bird’s-eye grid around the car is a query. It lifts itself into a short vertical pillar of 3-D points, projects those points into whichever cameras see them, and reads the image features there. It also reads its own previous state, so speed can be inferred.

What they found
  • With the time stream, nuScenes test NDS 0.569 vs 0.495 without it, and velocity error 0.378 vs 0.842 (Table 1).
  • Local deformable attention beat global attention (NDS 0.448 vs 0.404) and needed about 20 GB vs about 36 GB of GPU memory (Table 5).

For mobility: The grid cell asks, and geometry decides which pixels it may read: the same idea as the lane-anchor hub at the intersection.

V2X-ViT

Xu, Xiang, Tu et al. · ECCV 2022 · arXiv:2203.10638
Driving and V2X
Also: Figure 2 of the paper
Streams
LiDAR features from several agents, connected vehicles and roadside infrastructure, in the simulated V2XSet dataset.
Where they meet
After each agent’s own PointPillar encoder; shared features are compressed, sent, and warped to the ego vehicle’s pose.
Who asks
At each grid location, every agent asks every agent, itself included.
One softmax?
One softmax over the agents at the same spatial position (HMSA).
Stream tag
Agent type enters through type-specific weights and edge types (vehicle–vehicle, vehicle–infrastructure, …), not an added vector. A delay-aware position code adds each agent’s time lag.

Cooperative perception with the problems a V2X engineer knows: messages arrive late, poses are a little wrong, and a roadside LiDAR is not a car. The model stamps each agent’s features with its delay, treats the two agent types with different weights, and uses windows of several sizes to absorb position errors.

What they found
  • With 0.2 m pose noise and 100 ms delay, AP@0.7 of 0.614 vs 0.541 for DiscoNet and 0.402 with no fusion (Table 1).
  • Adding the type-aware attention raised AP@0.5/0.7 from 0.786/0.548 to 0.823/0.601 (Table 2).

For mobility: A direct template for fusing what vehicles and roadside units share, with latency and localization error built in.

Wayformer

Nayakanti, Al-Rfou et al. (Waymo) · ICRA 2023 · arXiv:2207.05844
One sequenceDriving and V2X
Streams
Agent history, interactions with other agents, the road graph, and traffic-light states, for motion forecasting.
Where they meet
Compared three ways: early (one encoder over all), late (one encoder per stream, meeting only in the decoder), and hierarchical (both).
Who asks
In the encoder, every scene token (or a set of latent queries); in the decoder, learned trajectory queries ask the fused scene.
One softmax?
Early fusion: one softmax over all four streams.
Stream tag
Learned position embeddings for all streams; no separate stream-type vector is described.

A deliberately simple design: project each stream to one width, concatenate, and let attention do the rest. The paper’s main experiment is the fusion choice itself, across model sizes and latency budgets.

What they found
  • Small models did best with early fusion; under 16 ms latency late fusion was the better choice; with more capacity the choice mattered less (Section 5.1).
  • Latent queries sped up all fusion variants 2× to 16× with little or no loss in quality; the leaderboard model uses early fusion.

For mobility: The transportation example of the mainstream recipe: map, signals and road users as tokens in one sequence.

BEVFusion

Liu, Tang et al. (MIT) · ICRA 2023 · arXiv:2205.13542
Driving and V2X
Streams
Six surround cameras and LiDAR, for 3-D detection and map segmentation.
Where they meet
After both streams are bird’s-eye-view maps: the camera features are lifted into 3-D with a predicted depth for each pixel, the LiDAR is flattened.
Who asks
Nobody: the two maps are concatenated and passed through a convolutional encoder.
One softmax?
No attention at all.
Stream tag
Not needed: position is the grid cell itself.

If you can put every sensor on the same map, the map does the matching. Most of the engineering went into making the camera-to-map step fast.

What they found
  • Map segmentation mIoU 62.7 with both sensors vs 56.6 camera-only and 48.6 for a LiDAR-only model (Table III).
  • 253.2 GMACs and 119.2 ms vs 485.8 GMACs and 156.6 ms for TransFusion (Table I).

For mobility: When geometry can align the streams (calibrated cameras and LiDAR on one vehicle or pole), you may not need attention to fuse them.

BLIP-2

Li, Li, Savarese & Hoi · ICML 2023 · arXiv:2301.12597
Queries and bottlenecksBridges to frozen models
Also: Figure 2 of the paper
Streams
Images and text; a frozen image encoder and a frozen language model.
Where they meet
In the Q-Former, a small trainable transformer between the two frozen models.
Who asks
32 learned queries ask the frozen image features through cross-attention, inserted every other block.
One softmax?
Separate cross-attention to the image; queries and text share self-attention layers under masks that change with the training objective.
Stream tag
The queries are their own learned tokens; no stream-type vector is described.

The 32 query outputs (32 × 768) are far smaller than the image encoder’s output (257 × 1024 for ViT-L/14). A linear layer projects them to the language model’s width, and they are put in front of the text as “soft visual prompts”.

What they found
  • Zero-shot VQAv2 65.0 with 108 M trainable parameters vs 56.3 for Flamingo-80B with 10.2 B (Table 2).

For mobility: Summarizing a large, frozen camera model into a few tokens a language model can read, for example for incident reports from CCTV.

LLaVA

Liu, Li, Wu & Lee · NeurIPS 2023 · arXiv:2304.08485
One sequenceBridges to frozen models
Streams
An image and a text instruction; output is text.
Where they meet
At the language model’s input: image tokens and text tokens enter one sequence.
Who asks
Every token, in the language model’s own causal self-attention.
One softmax?
One softmax over image and text tokens; a causal mask lets each token read only earlier tokens.
Stream tag
No type vector is described: a learned projection maps image features into the word-embedding space.

A pretrained CLIP vision encoder, one trainable projection matrix, and a pretrained language model (Vicuna). Stage 1 trains only the projection; stage 2 also trains the language model. The authors name Flamingo’s gated cross-attention and BLIP-2’s Q-Former as alternatives they leave for future work.

What they found
  • ScienceQA 90.92; skipping the stage-1 alignment cost 5.11 points (Table 8).

For mobility: The cheapest bridge from a camera model to a language model: a starting point for question answering over traffic-camera images.

Chameleon

Chameleon Team · Technical report (Meta) · arXiv:2405.09818
One sequence
Streams
Images, text and code; it can both read and generate images.
Where they meet
Early: “all modalities are projected into a shared representational space from the start”.
Who asks
Every token, causally.
One softmax?
One softmax; all weights shared across modalities.
Stream tag
Start-of-image and end-of-image tokens; no type vector. A 512 × 512 image becomes 1,024 tokens from an 8,192-entry codebook.

No separate vision encoder at inference time: an image tokenizer turns each image into discrete tokens, like words, and one model reads and writes both.

What they found
  • One shared softmax brought a stability problem: “each modality will try to compete with the other by increasing its norms”. Without a fix (QK-Norm), the 7B model diverged after about 20% of a training epoch.

For mobility: A warning for one-pool designs with very different streams: watch for one stream crowding the others out, as on the token-count slide.

The standard architecture

Put the fifteen side by side and one recipe accounts for most of them. Here it is, drawn for one mobility task: will the driver take over from ADAS in the next few seconds, judged from the road camera, the driver camera, CAN, V2X messages and the route.

What almost every paper does

  1. An encoder per stream, often pretrained and sometimes frozen: a ViT or CNN for cameras, PointPillar or a voxel network for LiDAR, a language model for text. (ViLT, MulT, Perceiver, Wayformer and Chameleon keep the per-stream step to a projection or a tokenizer.)
  2. A projection to one shared width, so tokens from different streams can sit in the same attention: LLaVA’s single matrix, Wayformer’s projection layer, BLIP-2’s fully connected layer.
  3. Something that says where each token came from: a stream-type vector (ViLT), a modality code (Perceiver), type-specific weights (V2X-ViT), marker tokens (Flamingo, Chameleon) or simply separate blocks per stream (ViLBERT, MulT). Plus position, and in driving, time: V2X-ViT’s delay code, BEVFormer’s previous map.
  4. Attention as the meeting point, built in one of four ways, below.
  5. Task queries or a summary token that hold the answer: a class token, BEV grid cells, trajectory queries, the next text token.

The standard cross-attention block

CrossAttn(Xq, Xkv) = softmax( (XqWQ)(XkvWK)T / √d ) · XkvWV
SymbolMeaningExamples from the papers
Xqthe asking tokensBEV grid cells (BEVFormer), latents (Perceiver), 32 queries (BLIP-2), text tokens (Flamingo), trajectory queries (Wayformer)
Xkvthe answering tokens: one or more streamscamera features, LiDAR, the 64 visual tokens of Flamingo’s Resampler
WQ, WK, WVlearned projectionsseparate per stream in ViLBERT and MulT; shared in one-sequence models
dwidth of one headthe √d keeps the scores from growing with the width

In words: each asking token scores every answering token, the softmax turns the scores into weights that add to 1, and the token takes the weighted average of what comes back. In practice the block sits inside a residual layer, x ← x + CrossAttn(LayerNorm(x), streams), followed by an MLP, and often after a self-attention step among the asking tokens: the decoder pattern of DETR, BEVFormer and the Perceiver. Flamingo multiplies the result by tanh(α) before adding it; that is a gate.

Self-attention over one sequence is the same equation with Xq = Xkv = all tokens. That is why the one-sequence designs need no separate cross-attention: every row of their attention is a cross-attention over every stream at once, and each row splits exactly: the weight on a token = the share of its stream × its weight within that stream. So the split between streams can be read out of any of them.

What still varies, and how to choose

QuestionOptionsSeen inChoose by
Where do the streams first meet?early · mid · lateViLT, Chameleon · ViLBERT, MBT, TransFuser · CLIPWayformer: early fusion is best for small models, late fusion under tight latency; MBT: mid beat both. Test it.
Who asks?every token · a few queries · one streamLLaVA · Perceiver, BEVFormer, BLIP-2 · Flamingo (text asks)whatever your output is indexed by: one answer per grid cell, per trajectory, per text token
One softmax across streams, or one per stream?shared · separateViLT, TransFuser, V2X-ViT · ViLBERT, MulT, Flamingoshared lets streams compete and gives a readable split; separate keeps streams apart and allows gates
How is cost kept down?latents · bottleneck tokens · geometry · local attentionPerceiver, Wayformer · MBT · BEVFormer, BEVFusion · BEVFormer, V2X-ViTthe number of tokens: cameras produce far more than anything else
How do you add a stream to a model that already works?gated layers · learned queries · a projectionFlamingo · BLIP-2 · LLaVAhow much you can retrain, and how much you must not disturb

How the practice moved

2019: two towers that trade keys and values (ViLBERT), or one block per pair of streams (MulT). 2021: one sequence with a type tag (ViLT), latent arrays and bottlenecks to tame the cost (Perceiver, MBT), and contrastive two-tower training for retrieval (CLIP). 2022–2023: bridges from frozen pretrained models: gated cross-attention (Flamingo), learned queries (BLIP-2), a single projection (LLaVA). 2024: everything as tokens from the start (Chameleon). In driving, geometry has stayed central throughout: BEV grids whose cells ask the cameras (BEVFormer), maps that align sensors before they meet (BEVFusion), and V2X features warped to the ego vehicle’s pose (V2X-ViT).

Check yourself

1. A city wants to fuse camera, loop and BSM data at 200 intersections, on roadside computers with tight latency. Which two papers would you read first, and why?

Wayformer (it measured how the fusion choice changes with latency: late fusion won under 16 ms) and BEVFusion or BEVFormer (geometry aligns sensors cheaply when they are calibrated to one map). A Perceiver-style latent hub is the third candidate if the camera tokens dominate the cost.

2. Your team has a validated road-camera takeover model and wants to add the driver camera without retraining everything. Which design fits?

Flamingo’s: new cross-attention layers, with the road side asking the driver camera, each scaled by a tanh gate that starts at 0, so the validated model is unchanged at first. BLIP-2’s learned queries are the alternative if the driver-camera encoder is large and frozen.

3. TransFuser’s authors found that in the early fusion stages LiDAR tokens barely attend to the image, while in the later stages nearly all do. What does that tell you, and what does it not?

It says the model reads across streams more in its deeper stages, which fits MBT’s finding that mid fusion works well. It does not prove the image information is used there. To test that, remove the image stream and watch the output.
